title: Macquarie turns to term deposits
full_text:
Macquarie has been winning market share in household deposits from the big four retail banks by offering simple products with competitive interest rates and no strings attached. It will now apply the same strategy to the $320 billion term deposit market, a key source of funding for major lenders.
The financial services giant has already snared a 6.4 per cent share of the total $1.7 trillion of household deposits with its "no hoops" savings account that pays interest without conditions, but until now has been a minor player in term deposits.
"We are underweight in term deposits, so there is plenty of room for us to grow, balance out diversification of the deposit book [and] increase the pool of deposits," said Olivia McArdle, head of deposits and payments at Macquarie Bank. "This is a little-talked-about space that hasn't had any innovation for years."
Macquarie holds $4 billion in term deposits - just 3.5 per cent of its total household deposit balance of $112 billion as of the end of May.
The bank's savings and transaction account strategy has raised awareness about sometimes sneaky terms and conditions used by the majors - such as requiring a minimum deposit to trigger bonus interest rates - and large balances held in transaction accounts at big banks on which no interest is paid.
Under Macquarie's new term deposit offering, there will be no automatic rollovers when terms expire. These can catch customers out, as some banks send funds not rolled over into holding accounts that pay no interest. Nor will there be break fees if customers decide to withdraw early, and they will earn the interest accrued up to the day they provide 31 days' notice.
The bank will also bring its term deposit business, which was previously run on a separate manual system, on to its main digital distribution system, which McArdle said should help to drive stronger sales growth by allowing customers to shift funds at the push of a button.
The move is set to lift competitive pressure in the hotly contested deposit market - the cheapest source of funding for banks and a key battleground to win sticky customers - at a time when lower credit growth from property tax changes in the federal budget is expected to reduce deposit growth and crimp margins this financial year.
As major banks prepare to deliver financial results next month, analysts say deposit competition will be a key focus given credit growth is slowing after the budget's tax changes put the brakes on the mortgage market. Some predict deposit growth will slow faster than lending, suggesting Macquarie could exert outsized pressure.
"In an environment of scarcer deposits, we expect banks to compete more aggressively for a smaller pool of funding, compressing deposit spreads and therefore profitability," said Jefferies analyst Andrew Lyons.
Commonwealth Bank has 31 per cent of its total deposits in term deposits, compared to 39 per cent in its savings products, 12 per cent in transaction accounts and 18 per cent in mortgage offsets. ANZ and National Australia Bank have 19 per cent of deposits as term deposits, with Westpac at 17 per cent, according to Jefferies.
The pressures being exerted by Macquarie can be seen in official statistics from the prudential regulator. Its latest data, published on June 30, showed Commonwealth Bank went backwards in total household deposits in the month of May. It is still the largest, though, with $461.7 billion, for a 26.5 per cent market share.
Over the past 12 months, CBA, Westpac and NAB's deposit books have been flat, while ANZ has lost 37 basis points of market share. Macquarie is up by 1.32 percentage points.
With interest rates possibly nearing a peak, competition to offer term deposits that lock in rates is picking up. A total of 13 banks increased term deposit rates last week by an average of 0.28 percentage points, according to Canstar. The maximum 12-month term deposit rate is 5.55 per cent and the average rate is 5.15 per cent.
"This upward pressure on term deposit rates reflects a market where competitive forces for household deposits and the possibility of at least one more cash rate hike is pushing some banks to increase their offers," said Sally Tindall, director of data insights at Canstar.
Macquarie, which requires a minimum $25,000 balance in a term deposit, higher than other banks, will offer a 12-month interest rate of 5.2 per cent, just below CBA's current 12-month rate of 5.25 per cent. But for three months, Macquarie will pay 5 per cent compared to CBA's 3.35 per cent. Term deposit rates are reset regularly based on funding costs in financial markets.
"We don't need to be that top rate; we want to be there or thereabouts," said McArdle. "It will ebb and flow depending on what the forward rate is doing. And what we're seeing, at the moment, for the next 12 months, is that the forward is quite flat.
"We see customers increasingly tuning in to what rate they're getting on deposits. For us, that can only be a benefit. We are providing a competitive offering - whether it be a savings account or a term deposit - making it really clear and transparent what the rate they're getting, and making it easy for them to switch."
